sections.title: Server File Transfer at Ames
sections.content:
Wayne Hathaway describes the initial Server File Transfer implementation at NASA Ames Research Center under TSS/360. The RFC also comments on the current File Transfer Protocol and suggests possible extensions.

The server follows TSS file-management conventions, so the document explains relevant user IDs, catalogs, dataset names, and sharing before describing FTP commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The server connects network file transfer to the files and catalogs already used by TSS. The RFC describes that site's implementation.

sections.title: TSS Catalogs and File Structure
sections.content:
Each TSS user has a user ID and a catalog containing pointers to datasets. Dataset names can have several qualification levels, and catalogs can include entries that share another user's dataset.

TSS files have record structure. For structured transfers, the server adds or expects an end-of-record sequence; for unstructured transfers, it does not add one when sending.
sections.plainLanguage: A TSS catalog is a user's directory of dataset entries. The server must account for whether transferred data is divided into records or treated as a stream.

sections.title: Commands and Transfer Choices
sections.content:
The RFC describes how FTP commands such as USER, RETR, STOR, APPE, DELE, and STAT act on TSS datasets. It notes that some commands need an active user, while MAIL and MLFL can be used before a USER command.

The server supports ASCII and IMAGE data types and describes how transfer mode and structure affect record endings and stored files.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP commands become TSS actions such as retrieving, storing, appending, deleting, or listing datasets. The chosen transfer type and structure affect how the data is saved.
